y-m-60-01.title: Only one solution? Where did the work go wrong?
y-m-60-01.topic: Properties of logarithms and the argument condition: the solutions of log₂(x²)=4
y-m-60-01.goal: Learn that a step using a logarithm property can change the allowed range of x, find the line where solutions disappear and fix it, and pick out the steps that do not change the range.
y-m-60-01.material: Suho solved the equation log₂(x²) = 4 (x is a nonzero real number) as shown below. (How to read: log₂ A is 'the logarithm of A with base 2', and x² is 'x squared'.)
y-m-60-01.thinking.0: Check whether each line holds under the same conditions as the line before it
y-m-60-01.thinking.1: Check the solutions by substituting them directly
y-m-60-01.thinking.2: Compare the allowed range before and after a transformation
y-m-60-01.prereq.0: The definition and properties of logarithms (the argument must be positive, and log M^k = k·log M is used when M>0)
y-m-60-01.prereq.1: The relationship between numbers whose absolute value and square are the same
y-m-60-01.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have already learned the properties of exponents and logarithms.
y-m-60-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Suho's solution where it goes wrong.
y-m-60-01.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether each line holds for the same range of x as the line before it.
y-m-60-01.s.s1.hint.1: Plug one negative x into the original equation and check whether the value is defined.
y-m-60-01.s.s1.line.4: So the only solution is x = 4.
y-m-60-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is where it goes wrong. log₂ x can be used only when x is positive, but the original equation still makes sense when x is negative, because x² is positive. Line 2 leaves out the case x<0, and as a result the claim 'only one' in line 5 is a wrong conclusion. Line 5 is also accepted as a wrong line. Even x = −4 gives log₂ 16 = 4.
y-m-60-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two different real numbers x that satisfy the original equation log₂(x²) = 4.
y-m-60-01.s.s2.hint.0: Using the definition of a logarithm, rewrite log₂ A = 4 as a relationship between A and 2.
y-m-60-01.s.s2.hint.1: Plug the x you found into the original log₂(x²) and check that you get 4.
y-m-60-01.s.s2.fail.c1: If x=0, then x²=0, so the argument of the logarithm is not positive.
y-m-60-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The value of log₂(x²) is not 4. Think again about what power of 2 gives x².
y-m-60-01.s.s2.explain: By the definition of a logarithm, x² = 2⁴ = 16, so x = 4 or x = −4. Both values satisfy the original equation, so there are two solutions.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.prompt: A transformation like Suho's line 2 can change the allowed range of x. Choose all the transformations below where 'the range of values x can take is the same before and after'. (x is a real number.)
y-m-60-01.s.s3.hint.0: For the left and right side of each option, write separately 'what range x must be in for the value inside the logarithm to be positive', and compare them.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.hint.1: For options where the ranges look different, plug one negative x into both sides.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.r.a: The right side makes sense only when x>0, while the left side needs only x≠0. Plug x=−4 into both sides.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.r.b: Compare whether the condition for x/3 to be positive is the same as the condition for x to be positive.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.r.c: The left side also makes sense for x<0 or x>2. Think about which range the right side makes sense in.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.r.d: The left side makes sense only for x>0, while the right side makes sense even when x is negative. The range got wider.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.r.e: The condition for |x| to be positive is the same as x≠0. Check whether negative x is included.
y-m-60-01.s.s3.explain: For b, x/3>0 ⇔ x>0, so the range is the same, and for e, |x|>0 ⇔ x≠0, so the range is the same. In a, x<0 disappears; in c, the x<0 side disappears; and in d, the range gets wider the other way around. A transformation that changes the range can make you lose or gain solutions, so after transforming you must plug back into the original equation to check.

y-m-60-02.title: Is a bigger exponent always a bigger value?
y-m-60-02.topic: Comparing exponents: cases where the direction of the inequality depends on the base
y-m-60-02.goal: Learn that 'every example I checked works' is not enough evidence for a general claim, build a counterexample yourself, and pick out the conditions needed to reach a conclusion.
y-m-60-02.material: Minji said, "a is positive and a≠1. Then if aᵐ < aⁿ, then m < n." (m and n are real numbers. How to read: aᵐ is 'a to the m-th power'.) Minji checked that with a=2, 2¹ < 2³, and with a=3, 3² < 3⁵, and in both cases m<n.
y-m-60-02.thinking.0: Judge how representative the examples are (which range of bases was tested)
y-m-60-02.thinking.2: Pick out the conditions needed for the conclusion
y-m-60-02.prereq.0: Powers and the laws of exponents (including negative and zero exponents)
y-m-60-02.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the exponents and logarithms unit.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.prompt: Based on the two examples Minji checked, which statement about Minji's claim is the most appropriate?
y-m-60-02.s.s1.hint.0: Look at where in the possible range of a the values Minji tested are clustered.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one a from a range that was not tested and actually calculate aᵐ and aⁿ.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.o.a: It worked twice, with 2 and 3, so we can say the claim holds for every a
y-m-60-02.s.s1.r.a: Working twice is not a proof. First look at what range of numbers the tested bases come from.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.o.b: We can't be sure until we separately test cases where m and n are real numbers that are not integers
y-m-60-02.s.s1.r.b: The problem is the range of the base a rather than the range of m and n. Look again at the a values that were tested.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.o.c: The tested bases are all greater than 1, so we can be sure only after testing bases less than 1 too
y-m-60-02.s.s1.o.d: Examples that hold do not break the claim, so if no counterexample appears, we may accept it as true
y-m-60-02.s.s1.r.d: Never having looked for a counterexample is different from there being no counterexample. See which a values have not been tested yet.
y-m-60-02.s.s1.explain: The tested bases 2 and 3 are both greater than 1. Since a could also be 0<a<1, we can't say 'always' until we test that case. What range the checked examples represent decides how strong the evidence is.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.prompt: Make and enter two (a, m, n) with different bases a such that aᵐ < aⁿ but m>n. (a is a number greater than 0 and not equal to 1. You may write it as a decimal.)
y-m-60-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a to be a number less than 1, and calculate a few values to see how aᵐ changes as m gets larger.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a few integers for m and n, calculate a^m and a^n, and then compare their sizes.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a is greater than 0 and not 1.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be positive and not equal to 1.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.fail.c2: m is not greater than n. Choose two numbers with m>n.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.fail.c3: aᵐ is not less than aⁿ. Actually calculate both values and compare them.
y-m-60-02.s.s2.explain: For example, with a=0.5, m=3, n=1, we get 0.5³=0.125 < 0.5¹=0.5 even though m>n. With a=0.25, m=2, n=−1, we get 0.0625 < 4. Minji's claim does not hold for 0<a<1.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.prompt: From the fact that aᵐ < aⁿ, what else do you need to know, in addition to the condition above (a is positive, a≠1), to be able to conclude m < n? Choose all that are sufficient. (You can find out by building counterexamples and testing.)
y-m-60-02.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, look for an (a, m, n) that satisfies its condition and is still a counterexample.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.hint.1: For each option, check whether the remaining range of a contains numbers less than 1.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.o.a: The fact that a is a natural number
y-m-60-02.s.s3.r.a: If a is a natural number and not 1, think about where a starts. Write the smallest possible value.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.o.b: The fact that m and n are both positive
y-m-60-02.s.s3.r.b: a=0.5, m=3, n=1 has m and n both positive, yet aᵐ<aⁿ while m>n.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.o.c: The fact that a is greater than 1/2
y-m-60-02.s.s3.r.c: With a=0.7, m=3, n=1, we get 0.343<0.7 even though m>n.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.o.d: The fact that a is greater than 1
y-m-60-02.s.s3.r.d: If a is greater than 1, aˣ only changes in the increasing direction, so the direction of the inequality is kept.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.o.e: The fact that a≠1 (a condition we already have)
y-m-60-02.s.s3.r.e: It is a condition we already know, so it is not new information. It does not tell a>1 and 0<a<1 apart.
y-m-60-02.s.s3.explain: If a>1, aˣ is increasing, so aᵐ<aⁿ ⇒ m<n. If a is a natural number other than 1, then a≥2, so a>1, which is also sufficient. For b, c, and e, values of a with 0<a<1 remain, so a counterexample is possible. By the way, if 0<a<1 were known, the conclusion would be m>n instead.

y-m-60-03.title: How many digits of an approximation can we trust?
y-m-60-03.topic: Approximations of common logarithms and number of digits: how far can we trust an approximation?
y-m-60-03.goal: Learn that a small error in an approximation can change the conclusion as n gets large, find cases where the conclusion differs, and state the conditions under which an approximation can be trusted.
y-m-60-03.material: We want to find how many digits 2ⁿ has. The number of digits of a positive integer N is (the integer part of log N) + 1, so the number of digits of 2ⁿ is (the integer part of n × log 2) + 1. The actual value of log 2 is 0.30102999566…, but Soyoung used the approximation 0.301 and found the number of digits by adding 1 to the integer part of n × 0.301. (The integer part is the integer before the decimal point. Example: the integer part of 9.03 is 9.)
y-m-60-03.thinking.0: Consider the effect of the error on the conclusion
y-m-60-03.thinking.1: Find cases where the conclusion differs yourself
y-m-60-03.thinking.2: State the conditions under which it can be trusted
y-m-60-03.prereq.0: The relationship between common logarithms and the number of digits (the number of digits of a positive integer N is the integer part of log N plus 1)
y-m-60-03.prereq.1: The fact that the value of log 2 is about 0.301, and using a calculator
y-m-60-03.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the common logarithms unit.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.prompt: For n=30, Soyoung said 30 × 0.301 = 9.03, so 2³⁰ is a 10-digit number. Can we trust this conclusion? Multiply 30 by the actual value 0.30102999566…, compare, and choose.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the value of 30 times the approximation and the value of 30 times the actual value side by side, to four decimal places.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the difference between the two values with the distance from the calculated value to the nearest integer.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.o.a: Since an approximation was used there is an error, so we can't know the number of digits until we calculate with the exact value
y-m-60-03.s.s1.r.a: The actual value is already given, so comparing the two products tells you the size of the error. Think about whether the error is big enough to change the conclusion.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.o.b: 9.03 is farther from the integer 9 than the error (less than 0.001), so the 10-digit conclusion holds
y-m-60-03.s.s1.o.c: The approximation is smaller than the actual value, so the actual number of digits is always one more than the number found with the approximation
y-m-60-03.s.s1.r.c: A slightly smaller value does not necessarily change the integer part. Think about what would have to happen for the integer part to change.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.o.d: 0.301 and the actual value agree up to the third decimal place, so the number of digits is the same for any n
y-m-60-03.s.s1.r.d: The error grows n times when multiplied by n. Compare the case n=30 with a case where n is very large.
y-m-60-03.s.s1.explain: 30 × 0.30102999566… = 9.0309… and 30 × 0.301 = 9.03, so the difference is less than 0.001. Both values are between 9 and 10, so the integer part is 9 in both cases, and 2³⁰ is a 10-digit number (2³⁰ = 1073741824). Whether an approximation can be trusted depends on the size of the error and how far the calculated value is from an integer.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two different natural numbers n for which the number of digits of 2ⁿ found with Soyoung's method (using 0.301) and with the actual value (using 0.30102999566…) differ. (Number of digits = the integer part of n × log 2 + 1)
y-m-60-03.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate for several n and look for an n where the decimal part of n × 0.301 is very close to 1.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate a few values to see how the difference between n×0.301 and n×(actual value) changes as n gets larger.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number that is 1 or greater.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The numbers of digits found by the two methods differ.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers of digits found by the two methods are the same. Compare the integer parts of n×0.301 and n×0.30102999566.
y-m-60-03.s.s2.explain: With n=196, 196 × 0.301 = 58.996 has integer part 58, so it says 59 digits, but with the actual value, 196 × 0.30102999566… = 59.0018…, so the integer part is 59 and 2¹⁹⁶ is a 60-digit number. The same happens for n=299 (91 digits) and n=392 (119 digits). When the calculated value is just below an integer, a small error can make it cross or not cross the integer, and the conclusion changes.
y-m-60-03.s.s3.prompt: For n=30 we could trust the approximation, but not for the n you just found. In one or two sentences, write what separates the cases where the number of digits found with the approximation 0.301 can be trusted from the cases where it cannot.
y-m-60-03.s.s3.hint.0: For n=30 and n=196, write how far n×0.301 is from the nearest integer.
y-m-60-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare that distance with n×(actual value − 0.301).
y-m-60-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The error, when n is ..., ...
y-m-60-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that the error grows with n?
y-m-60-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that it is risky when the calculated value is just below (or above) an integer?
y-m-60-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check what you said with the n you found (for example, 196) or with the calculation for n=30?
y-m-60-03.s.s3.model.0: The error of the approximation is multiplied by n, so the larger n is, the larger the error. So when n×0.301 is very close to an integer, the error can make it cross or not cross the integer and change the number of digits, and when it is far from an integer, you can trust it.
y-m-60-03.s.s3.model.1: When the calculated value 9.03 is far from an integer, like for 30, the integer part does not change even with the error (about 0.001). When the calculated value is 58.996, very close to the integer 59, like for 196, a small difference changes the number of digits.
y-m-60-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It does not say the error grows with n, but it gets the key point by comparing the distance from the integer with the error.

y-m-60-04.title: If sin θ is 3/5, is cos θ determined uniquely?
y-m-60-04.topic: Relationships among trigonometric functions: the conditions under which cos θ and tan θ are determined when sin θ is given
y-m-60-04.goal: Show, by finding all possible values, that the sine value alone does not determine the cosine and tangent values uniquely, and pick out the extra information that fixes the values.
y-m-60-04.material: The angle θ is a general angle (it doesn't matter whether in radians or degrees) and sin θ = 3/5. Harin said, "Since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cos θ = 4/5 and tan θ = 3/4." (How to read: sin θ is 'sine theta', sin²θ is 'sine theta squared', and 3/5 is 'three fifths'.)
y-m-60-04.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is sufficient
y-m-60-04.thinking.1: Find all cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-60-04.thinking.2: Pick out the extra conditions that determine the conclusion
y-m-60-04.prereq.0: The definition of trigonometric functions for general angles and their signs in each quadrant
y-m-60-04.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the trigonometric functions unit.
y-m-60-04.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most appropriate judgment about Harin's conclusion?
y-m-60-04.s.s1.hint.0: Find the value of cos²θ, then count how many numbers have that value when squared.
y-m-60-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write which quadrants contain angles whose sin θ is positive.
y-m-60-04.s.s1.o.a: Correct. From sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cos θ = 4/5 and tan θ = 3/4 are determined
y-m-60-04.s.s1.r.a: Check whether there is only one number whose square is 16/25.
y-m-60-04.s.s1.explain: Since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cos²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos θ = 4/5 or −4/5. If sin θ>0, θ is in the first or second quadrant, so both cases are possible.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two different possible pairs of values (cos θ, tan θ) for an angle θ with sin θ = 3/5. (Write fractions as decimals. Example: 3/5 = 0.6)
y-m-60-04.s.s2.hint.0: First find cos²θ, then find all the values of cos θ that give it.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.hint.1: For each cos θ, calculate sin θ ÷ cos θ to find tan θ.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.fail.c1: It is not sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. sin²θ is 0.36. Check what the square of cos θ should be.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It satisfies tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.fail.c2: tan θ × cos θ is not equal to sin θ = 0.6. Find tan θ again.
y-m-60-04.s.s2.explain: If cos θ = 0.8, then tan θ = 0.6 ÷ 0.8 = 0.75, and if cos θ = −0.8, then tan θ = −0.75. These two are all the possibilities.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.prompt: We want to ask for extra information to choose between the two possibilities. Choose all the pieces of information below that, added to sin θ = 3/5, would determine (cos θ, tan θ) uniquely even if only that one were given.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.hint.0: Plug the two candidates (0.8, 0.75) and (−0.8, −0.75) into the condition of each option.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.hint.1: Separate the options that both candidates satisfy from the options that only one satisfies.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.r.b: Between 0 and π there are angles in both the first and second quadrants. See whether both candidates remain.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.o.c: The fact that cos θ + sin θ < 1
y-m-60-04.s.s3.o.d: The fact that θ is an angle in the first or second quadrant
y-m-60-04.s.s3.r.d: If sin θ>0, this is already known. Check whether it is new information.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.r.e: In both candidates, cos θ is not 0. Check whether it can tell the two apart.
y-m-60-04.s.s3.o.f: The fact that sin θ × cos θ > 0
y-m-60-04.s.s3.explain: The candidates are (0.8, 0.75) and (−0.8, −0.75). a: tan θ<0 is satisfied only by the second. c: cos θ + sin θ is 1.4 for the first and −0.2 for the second, so <1 is satisfied only by the second. f: sin θ × cos θ>0 means cos θ>0, so only the first satisfies it. b, d, and e are satisfied by both candidates, so they can't tell them apart.
y-m-60-04.prereq.1: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ

y-m-60-05.title: The repeating cycle of sea level: how much can the data tell us?
y-m-60-05.topic: Period of the sine function: how far a period can be determined from measurements taken at regular intervals
y-m-60-05.goal: Learn that data measured at sparse intervals cannot settle the period, adjust your judgment as more data arrives, and compare candidate models directly with the measurements.
y-m-60-05.material: We want to measure the sea level (m) at a harbor and express it with a formula of the form h(t) = 3 + 2·sin(2πt/T). t is the time (in hours) since 0 o'clock, and T is the period (in hours). The measurements are rounded to units of 0.1 m and may fluctuate by about ±0.2 m because of waves. The goal is to determine T. (How to read: 2πt/T is '2π t over T'.)
y-m-60-05.thinking.0: Consider the limits of the data (the measurement interval)
y-m-60-05.thinking.1: Adjust your judgment and confidence according to new data
y-m-60-05.thinking.2: Compare candidate models with the measurements
y-m-60-05.prereq.0: The period 2π/b and the amplitude of the function y = a·sin(bx) + c
y-m-60-05.prereq.1: Values of trigonometric functions in radians (set the calculator to radian mode to calculate)
y-m-60-05.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have learned the graphs of trigonometric functions.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the most reasonable judgment.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, compare which of the candidates you thought possible earlier the new data has ruled out.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one candidate period, calculate the height at the revealed times yourself, and match it against the measurements.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.info: These are values measured at 3-hour intervals. t=0: 3.0 m, t=3: 5.0 m, t=6: 3.2 m, t=9: 1.0 m. If T=12, the formula gives 3.0, 5.0, 3.0, 1.0 m respectively.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: With the current data, what is the most reasonable judgment about the period?
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.after: T=12 and T=2.4 give the same values at 3-hour intervals (t=0, 3, 6, 9). So from these four values alone, 12 is likely but hard to confirm. We need to measure at finer intervals.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The period is 12 hours. All four values fit well with the model T=12
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Values measured at 3-hour intervals can come out the same for shorter periods too. For example, calculate the values at t=3, 6, 9 when T=2.4.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 12 hours is likely, but shorter periods are also possible, so it is too early to be sure
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The period is 3 hours. Since the values were measured every 3 hours, that interval is the period
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The values differ: 3.0 at t=0 and 5.0 at t=3. If the period were 3, the same value would have to repeat.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There are only four data points, so we can say nothing about the period
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Narrowing down the candidates is possible. Think about which candidates conflict with the data.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.info: We measured again at 1-hour intervals from t=0 to 6: 3.0, 4.0, 4.7, 5.0, 4.8, 4.1, 3.2 m.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does the new data change your judgment?
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.after: We can see the height slowly rising and falling over the hours, so short periods that go back and forth several times within an hour are ruled out. However, 0 to 6 hours is close to half a cycle, so 12 hours still relies on the assumption that the shape is symmetric.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Short periods like T=2.4 are ruled out, and 12 hours becomes more believable
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is the same information as the 3-hour data, so nothing has changed
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: With 1-hour intervals, there are points that the 3-hour data did not have. Look at how the height changes each hour.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 3.0 appeared at both t=0 and t=6, so the period is 6 hours
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: At t=0 the height is rising, and at t=6 it is falling. Even with the same value, the direction of change is different.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We have seen only half a period (0 to 6 hours), so 12 hours is a guess that relies on the assumption of symmetry
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does this data change your judgment?
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Keep T=12. Assume the measurements just fluctuated because of waves
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: T=12 predicts 3.0 and 3.0, but the measurements are 2.6 and 2.2. There are two differences beyond the ±0.2 m fluctuation, and they are in a direction that keeps widening.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Since the value at t=24 is 2.2, the sine-shaped model itself is wrong
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The shape is right. The values in the first 6 hours followed the sine shape well. What needs to change is the value of the period T.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: T is shorter than 12. The height dropped below 3, so it repeats faster
y-m-60-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If T is shorter than 12, then by t=12 it has already gone past one full cycle and could give a value higher than 3.0. For example, calculate h(12) with T=11.5.
y-m-60-05.s.s1.reflect: How did treating 12 hours as a 'likely candidate' rather than 'confirming' it at the first data help in the last data? On the other hand, if you had confirmed 12 hours, which data would have shaken that idea?
y-m-60-05.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one candidate, plug t=12 into the formula, find h(12) with a calculator in radian mode, and compare it with the measurement.
y-m-60-05.s.s2.hint.1: Do the same calculation at t=24, and find the candidate for which both values are within ±0.2 m.
y-m-60-05.s.s2.explain: If T=12.4, then h(12)≈2.60 and h(24)≈2.21, which match the two measurements. T=12 gives 3.0 and 3.0, T=13 gives 2.07 and 1.35, and T=11.5 gives 3.54 and 4.04, so they can't explain both measurements at once. (In places like this harbor, where the water rises and falls about twice a day, the period is in fact slightly longer than 12 hours.)

y-m-60-06.title: If the first 40 were all prime, is it prime for every n?
y-m-60-06.topic: Conjectures about the general term of a sequence: is it evidence that many terms work?
y-m-60-06.goal: Learn that 'it holds for the first several terms' is not enough evidence for 'it holds for every term', find a counterexample yourself, and say what is needed to trust a rule.
y-m-60-06.material: About the sequence aₙ = n² − n + 41 (n is a natural number), Sian said, "From a₁ to a₁₀ we get 41, 43, 47, 53, 61, 71, 83, 97, 113, 131, and they are all prime. So aₙ is prime for every n!" (How to read: aₙ is 'a sub n', and n² is 'n squared'.) In fact, primes come out for every n from 1 to 40.
y-m-60-06.thinking.0: Judge the strength of the evidence
y-m-60-06.thinking.2: Say what grounds are needed for something to hold in general
y-m-60-06.prereq.0: The general term of a sequence and calculating the values of terms
y-m-60-06.prereq.1: The definition of a prime number, and divisors and multiples
y-m-60-06.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the sequences unit.
y-m-60-06.s.s1.prompt: From the fact that the values are all prime for n=1 to 10 (or up to 40), which is the most appropriate statement about Sian's claim 'prime for every n'?
y-m-60-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what it takes to make 'prime for every n' false: does even a single n do it?
y-m-60-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare side by side the fact that you checked 40 values of n with the fact that there are endlessly many n.
y-m-60-06.s.s1.o.e: No example that breaks it has appeared yet, so we treat it only as a tentative guess
y-m-60-06.s.s1.r.e: This is a thought that separates 'there is no counterexample' from 'it is true' and keeps the judgment tentative.
y-m-60-06.s.s1.explain: Ten or forty being right does not guarantee 'every n'. Even one counterexample breaks the claim, and to trust that it holds for every n there must be a reason (a proof).
y-m-60-06.s.s1.acc.0: Pointing out that having no counterexample is not a proof, and keeping it as a tentative guess, is also a sound judgment.
y-m-60-06.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two different natural numbers n for which aₙ = n² − n + 41 is not prime.
y-m-60-06.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a few n, calculate aₙ, and check whether it has a divisor other than 1 and itself.
y-m-60-06.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number that is 1 or greater.
y-m-60-06.s.s2.fail.c2: aₙ is prime. Try a different n.
y-m-60-06.s.s2.explain: If n=41, then a₄₁ = 41² − 41 + 41 = 41² = 1681, and if n=42, then a₄₂ = 1763 = 41 × 43. If n=45, it is 2021 = 43 × 47. Even when forty are right, it breaks at the 41st.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.prompt: The first 40 were prime, but it broke at the 41st. Now, to believe that a rule of some sequence 'holds for every n', what is needed other than checking a few examples? Write one or two sentences.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write in one sentence what happened at n=41, and write how it affects the words 'for every n'.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write what kind of explanation must exist, other than the number of cases you checked, for you to believe 'for every n'.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even if many examples are right, ...
y-m-60-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that no matter how many examples there are, a single counterexample can break it?
y-m-60-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say even one thing about what the grounds (a reason, a proof) for believing 'for every n' would look like?
y-m-60-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use the result for n=41 that you just found as grounds for what you said?
y-m-60-06.s.s3.model.0: Even if you check 40 examples, it can break at the 41st. So you can trust it only when you give a reason with a formula for why it always holds for every n, or prove it.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.model.1: Even a large number of checked cases is not enough. If even one counterexample appears, the rule is wrong, so you need to know the reason why it always works.
y-m-60-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It asked for a reason without using the word 'proof'.

y-m-60-07.title: Checking a solution that finds the general term from a formula for the sum
y-m-60-07.topic: Sum of a sequence and its general term: checking the first term when finding aₙ from Sₙ
y-m-60-07.goal: In a solution that finds the general term from the sum Sₙ, find where the assumption n≥2 is missing, check with concrete numbers, and build a formula for the sum yourself for which the first term does not need to be fixed separately.
y-m-60-07.material: For a sequence {aₙ}, the sum of the first term through the n-th term is Sₙ = n² + 2n + 3 (n is a natural number), and Eunwoo found the general term as shown below. (How to read: aₙ is 'the n-th term', Sₙ is 'the sum from the first term to the n-th term', and Sₙ₋₁ is 'the sum up to the (n−1)-th term'.)
y-m-60-07.thinking.0: Check the assumptions of the solution
y-m-60-07.thinking.1: Check the conclusion with concrete numbers
y-m-60-07.thinking.2: Build a formula that satisfies the conditions yourself
y-m-60-07.prereq.0: The relationship between the sum Sₙ and the general term aₙ of a sequence (Sₙ is the sum from the first term to the n-th term)
y-m-60-07.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the sequences unit.
y-m-60-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Eunwoo's solution where it goes wrong.
y-m-60-07.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the conclusion a₁ = 3 directly with the definition of S₁ (the sum from the first term to the first term).
y-m-60-07.s.s1.hint.1: Look at what Sₙ₋₁ becomes when you plug n=1 into the formula in line 1.
y-m-60-07.s.s1.line.3: So for every natural number n, aₙ = 2n + 1.
y-m-60-07.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the first term is a₁ = 3.
y-m-60-07.s.s1.explain: Line 1 holds only when n≥2. S₀ is not defined, so it can't be used for n=1. So 'every natural number n' in line 4 and a₁ = 3 in line 5 are wrong. The first term is a₁ = S₁ = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. The calculations in lines 2 and 3 (2n+1 for n≥2) are correct. Choosing any of line 1, line 4, or line 5 is accepted.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.prompt: Sₙ = pn² + qn + r (p, q, r are integers, p≥1), S₃ = 21, and the first term a₁ = S₁ is at least 1. In this case, find two different values of p for which the value obtained by plugging n=1 into the formula from aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ (for n≥2) equals S₁ (that is, cases where the first term does not need to be fixed separately), and enter them.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ directly for pn² + qn + r and simplify it into an expression in n.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the condition that makes the value of that expression at n=1 equal to S₁ = p + q + r.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.ok.c1: p, q, r are integers and p≥1.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p, q, r must be integers, and p must be at least 1.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The first term S₁ is at least 1.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.fail.c3: S₁ = p + q + r is less than 1.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The value of the formula for n≥2 at n=1 equals S₁.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.fail.c4: Plugging n=1 into the formula 2pn + (q−p) obtained for n≥2 gives p+q. Check what value r must be for this to equal S₁ = p+q+r.
y-m-60-07.s.s2.explain: Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ = 2pn + (q − p), and plugging in n=1 gives p + q. For this to equal S₁ = p + q + r, r = 0 is needed. Then S₃ = 9p + 3q = 21, that is, 3p + q = 7, and the integer pairs satisfying S₁ ≥ 1 are (p, q) = (1, 4), (2, 1), (3, −2). For example, if Sₙ = 3n² − 2n, then aₙ = 6n − 5 also works at n=1 (a₁ = 1).
y-m-60-07.s.s3.prompt: In one or two sentences, using at least one concrete value (number), write why it is wrong to use aₙ = 2n + 1 for every n in Eunwoo's Sₙ = n² + 2n + 3.
y-m-60-07.s.s3.hint.0: Look at what Sₙ₋₁ is when n=1 in Eunwoo's aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.
y-m-60-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write side by side the value of S₁ calculated directly and the value of 2n+1 at n=1.
y-m-60-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that a₁ equals S₁ to get 6?
y-m-60-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you show the mismatch by comparing with the value of 2n+1 at n=1?
y-m-60-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also say that this formula can be used only for n≥2?
y-m-60-07.s.s3.model.0: a₁ is S₁, so it is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, but plugging n=1 into 2n + 1 gives 3, so they differ. So this formula can be used only for n≥2, and the first term must be found separately.
y-m-60-07.s.s3.model.1: The first term is S₁ = 6. But plugging n=1 into aₙ = 2n+1 gives 3, so it is wrong. To use Sₙ₋₁, n must be at least 2, so n=1 must be checked separately.

y-m-60-08.title: Which of two saving plans comes out ahead?
y-m-60-08.topic: Comparing the growth of arithmetic and geometric sequences: a choice that changes with the time period
y-m-60-08.goal: Compare a plan that grows by a fixed amount each year with one that grows by a fixed rate, learn that which is better depends on the time period, and give advice to people in different situations while stating your assumptions.
y-m-60-08.material: There are two saving plans that both start with 100만 원. Plan A grows by 10만 원 at the end of each year. Plan B grows by 5% of the previous year's amount at the end of each year (the amount after n years is 100 × 1.05ⁿ 만 원). Do not consider tax, prices, or early withdrawal. n is the number of years that have passed. (How to read: 1.05ⁿ is '1.05 to the n-th power'.)
y-m-60-08.thinking.0: Compare how the two models grow
y-m-60-08.thinking.1: Find the point where the conclusion changes
y-m-60-08.thinking.2: Write conditional advice that fits the person
y-m-60-08.prereq.0: The general term of an arithmetic sequence aₙ = a + (n−1)d, and of a geometric sequence aₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹
y-m-60-08.prereq.2: This is a difficulty level for this task (H3), not a school-year assignment, and it assumes you have finished the sequences unit.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.prompt: After 10 years, which plan has more money? Calculate each and choose.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the amounts after 1 year and after 2 years for each plan.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the amount after 10 years for each and compare the sizes.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.o.a: B has more. The plan that grows by a rate swells faster from the start
y-m-60-08.s.s1.r.a: Calculate the amounts after 1 year and 2 years for both plans and first check which one is ahead.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.o.b: They are the same. After 10 years, the amounts of the two plans are almost equal
y-m-60-08.s.s1.r.b: Calculate the amount after 10 years for each and compare. Use a calculator to find what 100 × 1.05¹⁰ is.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.o.c: A has more. For now, the plan that grows by a fixed amount each year is ahead
y-m-60-08.s.s1.o.d: There is not enough information. Even though the starting amounts are the same, we need to know more
y-m-60-08.s.s1.r.d: All the information needed is already given. Plug into the formulas and calculate.
y-m-60-08.s.s1.explain: After 10 years, A is 100 + 10 × 10 = 200만 원 and B is 100 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ 162.9만 원, so A has more. After 1 year too, A is 110 and B is 105, so A is ahead. The plan that grows by a rate is not ahead from the start.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter three different years n in which B has more money than A. (After n years, A is 100 + 10n and B is 100 × 1.05ⁿ 만 원. You may use a calculator.)
y-m-60-08.s.s2.hint.0: Increase n by 10 at a time, calculate both amounts, and see how the gap changes.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.hint.1: Near the first n where B has more than A, check by changing n by 1 at a time.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number that is 1 or greater.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.ok.c2: After n years, B has more than A.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.fail.c2: After n years, B does not have more than A. Make n larger and calculate the two amounts again.
y-m-60-08.s.s2.explain: If n=27, then B ≈ 373.3만 원 and A = 370만 원, so B is ahead for the first time. If n=26, then B ≈ 355.5만 원 and A = 360만 원, so A still has more. For n of 27 or more, B keeps having more. If n=40, B ≈ 704만 원 and A = 500만 원.
y-m-60-08.s.s3.prompt: Haeun wants to save money to use in 12 years, and Doyun wants to save money to use in 40 years. Write, in one or two sentences each, which of A and B you would recommend to each of them, with your reasons. (Also state the assumption that tax and prices are not considered.)
y-m-60-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write down the amounts of A and B at 12 years and at 40 years, compare their sizes, and then write.
y-m-60-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put the turning point you just found (from which year B is ahead) into your reason for the recommendation.
y-m-60-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give different advice to Haeun and Doyun, and was the reason based on the calculation results (for example, B is ahead from year 27)?
y-m-60-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the assumptions (tax and prices are not considered, the interest rate does not change)?
y-m-60-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is it free of statements like 'B is always better' or 'A is always better' that ignore the time period?
y-m-60-08.s.s3.model.0: I recommend A for Haeun because she will use the money in 12 years. After 12 years, A is 220만 원 and B is about 180만 원. I recommend B for Doyun because after 40 years B is about 704만 원, which is more than A's 500만 원. I did not consider tax and prices.
y-m-60-08.s.s3.model.1: A is ahead for a short period and B is ahead for a long period. That is because A has more until year 26, and B has more from year 27. So I would tell Haeun, with 12 years, that A is better, and Doyun, with 40 years, that B is better. However, I assumed the interest rate does not change.
y-m-60-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It used the turning point at year 27 as its grounds, without concrete amounts.
